subtopic: Why real estate over architecture or finance
question: What draws you to studying real estate rather than a related field like architecture or pure finance?
lookingFor: Genuine motivation that distinguishes real estate from adjacent fields, grounded in real interest or exposure.

bullets: Show a specific understanding of what real estate study actually covers
Distinguish it clearly from architecture (design) and finance in isolation
Ground the answer in a real experience or observation, not a general claim
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've always been fascinated by how a piece of land turns into a building people actually live and work in, and when I looked closer I realised that's not architecture, it's real estate, the decisions about location, financing, planning permission and who the building ends up serving. I did a weekend job at a local letting agency and saw how much analysis goes into working out whether a property is priced fairly, and that pulled me toward the more analytical side of the subject. Architecture designs the building and finance looks at the money on its own, but real estate sits in the middle, tying the physical asset to the market and the people who use it, and that combination is what I want to study.

commonMistakes: Confusing real estate with architecture or interior design
Giving a vague answer about 'liking houses'
Offering no personal grounding or experience
followUps: Which side interests you more, the development side or the investment side?

question: Why do you want to study real estate at this university specifically?
lookingFor: Specific, researched motivation for this programme, not generic praise that could apply anywhere.

bullets: Name a specific module, accreditation, placement year, or faculty focus
Connect it to a concrete personal interest or goal
Show you understand what makes this course different from a generic business or geography degree
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Your course is RICS-accredited and has a placement year built into the structure, and that combination matters to me because I want the professional qualification to actually mean something the moment I graduate, not something I chase separately afterwards. I read about the valuation module that uses live local case studies rather than textbook examples, and that hands-on approach is exactly how I learn best. I also liked that the course sits within a built environment faculty rather than pure business, because I want planning and construction context alongside the finance, and that's a mix I haven't found on other courses I looked at.

commonMistakes: Generic praise that would fit any university
Leaning only on rankings or reputation
Not knowing whether the course is accredited or what that means
followUps: What would you want to get out of a placement year if the course offers one?

question: Was there a specific moment or experience that first got you interested in real estate?
lookingFor: A genuine, specific origin story rather than a rehearsed or generic answer.

bullets: Describe one concrete moment or experience, not a vague lifelong interest
Explain what specifically caught your attention about it
Connect it forward to why you want to study the subject now
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My family moved house when I was fifteen, and I remember sitting in on the negotiation and being amazed at how much the final price shifted from the asking price once the survey flagged some structural issues. I started asking the agent questions afterwards about how she'd valued it in the first place, and she was patient enough to actually explain comparable sales to me. That was the first time I realised there was a whole discipline behind something I'd always thought was just a number on a sign, and I've been reading around it ever since.

commonMistakes: Claiming a lifelong interest with no specific trigger
Describing an experience with no reflection on what it revealed
Picking a moment that has nothing to do with real estate itself
followUps: What have you done since then to explore that interest further?

question: Tell us about any work experience or shadowing you've done related to real estate.
lookingFor: Real, reflected-on exposure to the industry, with evidence of what you learned rather than just where you were.

bullets: Name the specific experience and what you actually did day to day
Highlight one concrete thing it taught you about the industry
Be honest if experience is limited, and show initiative you took instead
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I spent a week shadowing a chartered surveyor doing residential valuations, and I got to sit in on three inspections and watch how she compared each property against recent sales nearby to justify her figure. What surprised me was how much of the job was actually about communicating a decision clearly to a nervous seller, not just the number crunching. I couldn't get a longer placement, so I followed it up by reading the RICS Red Book summary to understand the standards behind what I'd watched her do.

commonMistakes: Listing where you went without describing what you actually did
No reflection on what the experience taught you
Pretending to more experience than you actually have
followUps: What surprised you most about how the industry actually works day to day?

question: What have you read recently about the property market or the real estate industry?
lookingFor: Evidence of genuine, self-directed reading beyond the school syllabus, with the ability to discuss it.

bullets: Name a specific article, report, or book, not a vague 'the news'
Summarise the main point in your own words
Add your own reaction or a question it left you with
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've been reading a Savills market report on build-to-rent housing, which argued that institutional investors are moving into rental housing at scale because it offers steadier long-term returns than a lot of commercial property right now. What struck me was the idea that this could actually professionalise a rental market that's often quite fragmented and landlord-by-landlord. It left me wondering how tenants themselves feel about renting from a large fund rather than an individual landlord, which is something I'd like to look into more.

commonMistakes: Vague reference to 'the news' with no specific source
Summarising without any personal reaction or opinion
Reading only headlines without understanding the underlying argument
followUps: Do you agree with the argument it made? Why or why not?

question: What's happening in the housing market in your local area at the moment?
lookingFor: Genuine local awareness with some attempt to explain the cause, not just an observation.

bullets: State a specific, current observation about local prices, supply, or demand
Offer a plausible explanation for why it's happening
Show it comes from your own noticing, not a rehearsed line
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: In my town, terraced houses near the new train link have gone up noticeably in the last two years, while flats further out have barely moved. I think it's because the improved commute has made the area attractive to people who work in the city but couldn't previously afford to live close to a station, so demand has concentrated on that specific type of property near the line. I noticed it partly because a house two doors from us sold for well above what a similar one went for three years ago.

commonMistakes: A generic national statistic with no local specificity
No attempt to explain the cause
Confusing correlation with an unexamined guess presented as fact
followUps: What effect do you think that trend is having on people already living there?

question: Can you explain the difference between freehold and leasehold ownership?
lookingFor: A clear, accurate grasp of a basic property law concept, stated in plain language.

bullets: State that freehold means owning the property and the land outright, indefinitely
State that leasehold means owning the right to occupy for a fixed term, with the freeholder retaining the underlying land
Mention a practical implication, such as leases running down or ground rent
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Freehold means you own the building and the land it sits on outright, with no time limit on your ownership. Leasehold means you own the right to use the property for a set number of years, maybe ninety-nine or nine hundred and ninety-nine, while someone else, the freeholder, still owns the underlying land and can charge ground rent or service charges. The practical issue with leasehold is that as the number of years remaining falls, especially under about eighty years, the property can become harder to mortgage or sell, so buyers need to check the lease length carefully.

commonMistakes: Reversing the two definitions
Describing leasehold as if it were simply renting
Giving no practical implication of the difference
followUps: Why might a leasehold flat with sixty years left be harder to sell than one with two hundred?

question: In simple terms, what is a capitalization rate, or 'cap rate', and why does it matter to an investor?
lookingFor: A correct, plain-language grasp of a core investment concept with an explanation of its use.

bullets: Define cap rate as annual net operating income divided by property value
Explain that it's used to compare returns across different properties or markets
Note that a lower cap rate generally implies a safer or more sought-after asset
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A cap rate is the annual net income a property generates, after running costs but before mortgage payments, divided by what the property is worth or was bought for. It lets an investor compare two very different properties on the same footing, almost like a yield, to see which one is generating a better return relative to its price. Generally a lower cap rate signals a safer, more desirable asset, like prime city-centre offices, while a higher cap rate often reflects more risk or a less liquid market, so investors use it as a quick, comparable sense-check before digging into the details.

commonMistakes: Confusing cap rate with mortgage interest rate
Forgetting to net out operating costs from income
No explanation of what the number is actually used for
followUps: If two similar buildings have very different cap rates, what might that tell you?

question: How would you explain, using supply and demand, why house prices in a city might be rising?
lookingFor: A clear application of a basic economic concept to a real property market situation.

bullets: Identify a plausible demand-side driver, such as population or job growth
Identify a plausible supply-side constraint, such as limited land or slow planning approvals
Connect the two to explain the price effect, not just state the theory
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: If a city is adding jobs faster than it's adding new homes, more people are competing for a roughly fixed number of properties, and prices get bid upward. On the supply side, cities often can't easily build more, planning permission takes time, land close to the centre is scarce, and construction itself is slow, so supply can't respond quickly even when demand rises. That mismatch between fast-moving demand and slow-moving supply is usually the simplest explanation for sustained price growth in a city, rather than any single event.

commonMistakes: Stating the theory without applying it to a real scenario
Naming only a demand factor or only a supply factor
Confusing short-term price spikes with structural supply constraints
followUps: What could a city do to ease that kind of price pressure?

question: What's the difference between what a real estate developer does and what a real estate agent does?
lookingFor: A clear, accurate understanding of two distinct roles within the industry.

bullets: Describe a developer as someone who acquires land, finances, and builds or converts property
Describe an agent as someone who markets and sells or lets existing property on behalf of an owner
Note that a developer takes on much greater financial risk than an agent
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A developer buys land or an existing site, arranges financing and planning permission, and takes on the risk of actually building or converting the property, hoping to sell or let it at a profit once it's finished. An agent doesn't build anything, they're brought in to market a property that already exists, find a buyer or tenant, and negotiate the deal, usually earning a fee or commission for that. The developer is carrying construction and market risk over years, while the agent's role is much shorter and centred on the transaction itself.

commonMistakes: Treating the two roles as interchangeable
Describing an agent as someone who builds property
No mention of the difference in financial risk between the two
followUps: Which of those two roles sounds more appealing to you, and why?

question: Why has sustainability become such a major issue in real estate development?
lookingFor: Awareness of both the environmental and commercial drivers behind sustainability in the industry.

bullets: Mention that buildings account for a large share of carbon emissions
Note commercial pressure such as tenant demand, regulation, and stranded-asset risk
Show it's a genuine interest, not just a memorised talking point
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Buildings are responsible for a huge share of global carbon emissions, both from construction and from ongoing energy use, so real estate is one of the biggest levers available for tackling climate change. Beyond the environmental case, it's now a commercial issue too, tenants and investors increasingly want energy-efficient buildings, regulations are tightening minimum energy standards, and an inefficient building risks becoming a 'stranded asset' that's hard to let or sell. I find it interesting that sustainability has gone from a nice-to-have to something that directly affects a building's value.

commonMistakes: Treating sustainability as purely an ethical add-on with no commercial dimension
Vague statements with no specific driver named
Showing no awareness of regulation or stranded-asset risk
followUps: Can you name a specific sustainability feature you'd expect in a modern office building?

question: What do you understand by the term 'real estate cycle', and where do you think the market is in that cycle right now?
lookingFor: Basic conceptual understanding of cyclicality plus a willingness to venture a grounded, current view.

bullets: Describe the rough phases: recovery, expansion, oversupply or peak, and downturn
Explain that cycles are driven by the lag between demand shifts and supply responding
Offer a tentative, reasoned view on the current phase rather than refusing to answer
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The real estate cycle describes how markets move through phases, a recovery after a downturn, then expansion as confidence and rents rise, often followed by oversupply once too many developers respond to the same good news at once, and eventually a downturn as the market corrects. It happens because construction takes years, so supply can't adjust quickly to demand, which means the market tends to overshoot in both directions. My own reading suggests we're in a cautious, slow recovery phase in a lot of markets right now, with financing still expensive after higher interest rates, though I'd want to look at local data before being confident about any one city.

commonMistakes: Describing prices as moving in a straight line with no cyclicality
Refusing to venture any current view at all
Confusing the property cycle with the general business cycle without any real estate specifics
followUps: What signals would you look at to judge which phase a market is in?

question: How do rising interest rates typically affect property prices?
lookingFor: A correct causal explanation linking borrowing costs to affordability and valuation.

bullets: Explain that higher rates raise mortgage costs, reducing what buyers can afford to borrow
Note that higher rates also raise the discount rate used to value income-producing property, lowering valuations
Acknowledge it's not instant or uniform across all property types
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: When interest rates rise, mortgages get more expensive, so buyers can afford to borrow less for the same monthly payment, which tends to push demand and prices down, or at least slow growth. On the investment side, higher rates also make it more expensive to finance a purchase and raise the return investors expect elsewhere, so the price they're willing to pay for a given rental income tends to fall too. It doesn't happen instantly or evenly though, prime assets with strong tenants often hold up better than riskier or highly leveraged property.

commonMistakes: Only mentioning the mortgage-affordability channel and ignoring investment valuation
Claiming the effect is instant and uniform across all property types
Getting the direction of the relationship backwards
followUps: Would you expect all types of property to be affected equally? Why or why not?

question: What are some of the key differences between investing in commercial and residential property?
lookingFor: Understanding of at least two meaningful differences between the two asset classes.

bullets: Mention lease length differences, commercial leases are typically longer than residential tenancies
Mention that commercial income and value are more tied to business and economic conditions
Note differences in financing, liquidity, or entry cost between the two
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Commercial leases, like offices or retail units, tend to run for several years and often shift more of the running costs onto the tenant, while residential tenancies are usually much shorter and the landlord carries more of the maintenance burden. Commercial property values are also more sensitive to the health of businesses generally, an office building suffers if companies downsize, whereas people always need somewhere to live, so residential demand tends to be a bit steadier. Commercial property also usually needs more capital to get into and can be harder to sell quickly, so it suits a different kind of investor than a residential buy-to-let.

commonMistakes: Naming only one difference instead of comparing multiple dimensions
Assuming commercial and residential markets always move together
Confusing commercial property with new-build residential development
followUps: Which of the two do you find more interesting to study, and why?

question: The saying in real estate is 'location, location, location.' What factors actually make a location valuable?
lookingFor: Ability to break a well-worn phrase into specific, concrete drivers of location value.

bullets: Name concrete factors such as transport links, schools, employment access, or amenities
Distinguish factors that are fixed from ones that can change over time, like new transport links
Show the reasoning isn't just repeating the phrase but unpacking it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It usually comes down to things like how easily people can get to work from there, whether there are good schools nearby, and access to amenities like shops, parks or hospitals. Some of that is essentially fixed, you can't move a plot of land closer to the city centre, but some of it can change, a new train line or a big new employer opening nearby can transform a location's value over just a few years. I think that's actually one of the most interesting parts of the subject, spotting which currently unfashionable areas have the ingredients to become more valuable.

commonMistakes: Repeating the phrase without unpacking what 'location' actually means
Naming only one factor instead of several
Treating location value as entirely fixed and unchangeable
followUps: Can you think of an area near you that became more valuable because something changed?

question: Can you name a method used to value a property, and briefly explain how it works?
lookingFor: Correct, specific knowledge of at least one standard valuation method with a plain explanation.

bullets: Name one recognised method, such as the comparable method or the income method
Explain the mechanics in plain language
Mention when or why that method would be used
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: One common approach is the comparable method, where a valuer looks at recent sale prices of similar properties nearby, adjusts for differences like size, condition, or exact location, and arrives at a figure for the property in question. It's the method most people are familiar with because it's how residential valuations usually work, since comparable sales are relatively easy to find. For income-producing property like an office block, valuers often use the income method instead, capitalising the expected rental income at an appropriate yield, because there may not be enough directly comparable sales to rely on.

commonMistakes: Naming a method without explaining how it actually works
Confusing valuation with simply guessing a price
Describing a method for a property type it doesn't normally apply to
followUps: Why might the comparable method be harder to apply to a very unusual building?

question: What risks would you consider before investing in a rental property?
lookingFor: A structured, realistic view of the main risk categories an investor should weigh.

bullets: Cover at least two distinct risk types, such as void periods, tenant default, or maintenance costs
Mention market-level risk such as price falls or interest rate changes
Show a balanced, non-alarmist view rather than either dismissing or overstating risk
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: There's the tenant-level risk, void periods where the property sits empty earning nothing, or a tenant who stops paying rent and has to be evicted, both of which cost money and time. Then there's the property itself, unexpected repairs like a new roof or boiler can eat into returns quickly if you haven't budgeted for them. And there's market-level risk too, if interest rates rise and you have a mortgage on the property, or if prices fall in that area, your overall return can look very different from what you originally projected. I don't think any of that makes property a bad investment, but it does mean the numbers need a real cushion built in, not just the best-case rent.

commonMistakes: Naming only one type of risk instead of several
Being either unrealistically negative or dismissing risk entirely
Confusing risk with a simple list of costs
followUps: How would you build a margin of safety into your numbers to account for those risks?

question: How is technology changing the way property is bought, sold, or managed?
lookingFor: Awareness of real, specific examples of proptech rather than vague statements about 'digital' change.

bullets: Give at least one specific example, such as virtual viewings, online portals, or building management sensors
Explain the actual benefit it provides, not just that it exists
Show awareness that human judgement still matters alongside the technology
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Portals and virtual viewings have already changed how people search, buyers can filter and rule out a huge number of properties online before they ever visit in person, which saves everyone time. On the management side, sensors in commercial buildings can now track energy use and occupancy in real time, which helps landlords cut running costs and support sustainability goals I mentioned earlier. I don't think technology replaces the judgement a good agent or valuer brings, especially around things like negotiation or spotting a property's real condition, but it's clearly changing which parts of the job take up most of someone's time.

commonMistakes: Vague claims about 'digital transformation' with no concrete example
Overstating that technology will fully replace human roles in the industry
Naming an example but not explaining its actual benefit
followUps: Do you think technology will reduce the need for real estate agents? Why or why not?

question: Why do cities have zoning or planning laws, and how might they affect a developer?
lookingFor: Understanding of the public purpose of planning regulation and its practical effect on development.

bullets: Explain the public purpose, such as separating incompatible uses or protecting infrastructure capacity
Explain how planning rules constrain what a developer can build and where
Show balanced awareness that planning creates both friction and important protection
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Zoning and planning laws exist so that a city doesn't end up with, say, a factory built next to a school, and so that new development doesn't outpace the infrastructure, like roads or drainage, that has to support it. For a developer, that means before you can even think about construction you need to check what's permitted on that land, and getting permission for anything outside that can mean a lengthy and uncertain approval process, which adds real cost and risk to a project. I don't think that's necessarily a bad thing though, without those rules you'd probably get worse outcomes for the people who actually have to live near what gets built.

commonMistakes: Describing planning laws as pure bureaucratic obstruction with no public benefit
No mention of how it actually affects a developer's project timeline or cost
Confusing zoning with building safety regulations
followUps: Can you think of a case where planning rules and development interests might genuinely conflict?

question: New development often raises property values in a neighbourhood but can push out long-term residents. How should a developer think about that tension?
lookingFor: Structured ethical reasoning that weighs commercial reality against social consequence, not a one-line verdict.

bullets: Acknowledge both sides genuinely, investment benefits an area but can displace existing residents
Discuss concrete mitigations, such as affordable housing quotas or phased development
Avoid a glib answer that dismisses the tension in either direction
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I don't think there's a clean answer, investment genuinely can improve an area, better shops, safer streets, new jobs, but if rents rise faster than local incomes, the people who made the area worth investing in to begin with can end up being the ones who can't afford to stay. I think a responsible developer takes that seriously rather than treating it as someone else's problem, things like including a genuine proportion of affordable units, or phasing development so the local market isn't shocked all at once, are real levers rather than box-ticking. It's also not purely a developer's job to solve alone, local government policy on things like rent stabilisation or planning conditions matters just as much, but I wouldn't want to be part of a project that just assumed displacement was somebody else's problem.

commonMistakes: Dismissing the concern entirely as 'just how markets work'
Refusing to engage with the commercial reality at all
Giving a one-line verdict with no reasoning behind it
followUps: Should that responsibility fall on the developer, local government, or both? Why?

question: If a property costs 200,000 and rents for 12,000 a year, how would you work out its rental yield, and what does that number tell you?
lookingFor: Correct basic numeracy plus an understanding of what the resulting figure is used for.

bullets: Correctly calculate the yield as annual rent divided by price, expressed as a percentage
Arrive at approximately 6 percent
Explain what the figure is used for, comparing returns across properties
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: You'd divide the annual rent by the purchase price and multiply by a hundred, so twelve thousand divided by two hundred thousand comes to six percent. That figure is a gross yield, it gives a quick, comparable sense of the return the property generates before costs like maintenance, insurance or letting fees are taken out, so it's useful for comparing this property against other options at a glance. I'd want to also work out a net yield, taking running costs into account, before actually deciding whether it's a good investment, since the gross figure alone can be a bit optimistic.

commonMistakes: Getting the arithmetic wrong under pressure
Confusing gross yield with net yield and not noting the difference
Stating the number with no explanation of what it's used for
followUps: If annual maintenance and costs came to 2,000, what would the net yield be?

question: A client wants to buy a flat above a row of shops because it's cheap, but you notice the lease has only sixty years left. What would you want them to think about before buying?
lookingFor: Structured, practical reasoning that applies subject knowledge to a realistic client scenario.

bullets: Flag that a short lease affects mortgage availability and future resale value
Mention the cost and process of extending the lease as a factor in the real total cost
Frame the advice as informing the client's decision, not making it for them
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd want to make sure they understand that a lease under about eighty years can already make mortgages harder to get, and by the time they might want to sell it could be even shorter, which shrinks the pool of buyers who can get financing too. I'd point out that extending the lease is possible but usually isn't cheap, and that cost needs to be added to what looks like a bargain price to see the real total cost of ownership. Ultimately it's their decision, if they're planning to live there for decades and extend the lease early, it might still make sense, but I'd want them making that choice with the full picture rather than just seeing the low asking price.

commonMistakes: Not mentioning that short leases affect mortgage eligibility
Ignoring the cost of a lease extension as part of the real price
Telling the client what to do rather than informing their decision
followUps: How would you find out roughly what extending that lease might cost?

question: What role did real estate play in the 2008 global financial crisis, as far as you understand it?
lookingFor: A reasonably accurate, structured account of the connection between mortgage lending and the wider crisis.

bullets: Mention subprime mortgage lending and loose lending standards
Explain that mortgages were bundled into securities that spread the risk through the financial system
Note the effect, a housing price collapse that triggered a much wider banking crisis
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: As I understand it, lenders in the US had been issuing mortgages to borrowers with weak credit, so-called subprime loans, often on the assumption that rising house prices would cover any problems if the borrower defaulted. Those mortgages were bundled together into securities and sold on to investors around the world, which meant that when house prices stopped rising and defaults increased, the losses weren't contained to a few local lenders but spread through banks globally. It's a reminder to me that real estate isn't just a local market, it's connected to the wider financial system in ways that can amplify a problem far beyond where it started.

commonMistakes: Treating the crisis as purely a banking event unrelated to real estate
Vague statement that 'house prices crashed' with no explanation of the mechanism
Confusing the 2008 crisis with a different, unrelated downturn
followUps: Has anything changed in mortgage lending since then that you're aware of?

question: Have you come across the term REIT? What is it, and why might someone invest in one instead of buying property directly?
lookingFor: Correct basic knowledge of REITs and a clear explanation of the practical advantage they offer.

bullets: Define a REIT as a company that owns and often manages income-producing property, traded like a share
Explain the advantage of liquidity and lower entry cost compared to buying property directly
Mention diversification across many properties as another benefit
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A REIT, a real estate investment trust, is a company that owns a portfolio of income-producing properties, and instead of buying a building yourself you buy shares in that company, which then has to pass most of its rental income on to shareholders. The big advantage is that you can invest with a much smaller amount of money than buying a property outright, and you can sell your shares on the stock exchange almost instantly, whereas selling an actual building can take months. It also spreads your exposure across many properties rather than betting everything on one, which feels like a much lower-risk way to get real estate exposure as a smaller investor.

commonMistakes: Confusing a REIT with directly owning a rental property
Not mentioning liquidity as a key practical difference
Vague answer that doesn't explain what the acronym stands for or does
followUps: What might be a downside of investing through a REIT compared to owning property directly?

question: Real estate involves both hard numbers and dealing with people. Which of those do you think you're naturally stronger at, and how will you work on the other?
lookingFor: Honest self-assessment paired with a concrete, believable plan to develop the weaker area.

bullets: Give a genuine, specific answer rather than claiming to be equally strong at both
Back the claim with a real example
Describe a concrete step being taken to build the other skill
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'm naturally stronger on the numbers side, I enjoy maths and did well in economics, and I find the analytical part of valuation genuinely satisfying rather than a chore. The people side doesn't come as naturally to me, I can be quite reserved with people I don't know well, so I've been pushing myself to take on the role that involves the most client contact whenever I volunteer for group tasks at school, even when it's uncomfortable. I know real estate is ultimately a people business as much as a numbers one, so I don't want to end up hiding behind the analysis.

commonMistakes: Claiming to be equally strong at both with no real distinction
Naming a weakness with no evidence of actually working on it
Picking a weakness so severe it undermines the whole application
followUps: Can you give an example of a time you had to push yourself on the weaker side?
